[[RunningHead]]

The Psychic Space in Trauma

Norma Tracey

Norma Tracey

Sydney
11 Mars Road Lane Cove 2066 Sydney Australia

Norma Tracey  

“Her sullen resistance, which I had taken to be hostility, I now understood to be a dulling and deadening of her mind. The pall that fell over the sessions was a deadening in us both. I tried to show her she felt a need not to be aware, to make us both unthinking - she should not know me and I should not know her”.

Edna O'Shaughnessy (1981)

Introduction

I want to use this paper to think about an autistic, deadened, psychic space resulting from trauma. I begin with a statement and then attempt to give this statement meaning through theoretical constructs and case material.

Trauma is a psychic wound, caused by a violent intrusion. An excess of psychic pain floods the ego. Projective identification fails as a container. The psychic pain becomes unbearable and there is fear of fragmentation and death. Internal objects are destroyed, omnipotence takes their place, so there is no mourning. There is unthinkable fear, so there is no thinking, and hence no symbolization. The experience of negative feelings is greater than that of positive ones, causing archaic denial and regression to primary processing, instead of repression and secondary processing. What is left is a non-living space, where knowing would be it if could be known, where thought would be if it could be thought. This space has an autistic, deadening quality. Its cause is demonstrably similar to that described by Tustin (1972, 1981, 1988) in autistic children.

I will try to show how understanding this space has profound implications for therapy. I suggest there are specific, definable, therapeutic techniques by which this dead inner space may be restored to a psychic living experience. In therapy this deadened area becomes a space where agony previously avoided is tolerated, despair held, psychic pain of loss suffered and fear contained. Awareness of dosage and timing is all too relevant. Interpreting that focuses on love and hate or good and evil in the patient can be persecutory. The focus of the analytic therapy is on archaic denial and the fear, sometimes terror, of “knowing”. Psychic holding is the main therapist-patient interaction. If internal holding is no longer adequate because of the intensity of the trauma, external holding is necessary for its resolution.

Ill Treatment in the Counter Transference: Some Thoughts on Concurrent Work with an Adopted Girl and with Her Family by the Same Psychotherapist**

Trudy Klauber

Trudy Klauber

38 Holmdale Road
London NW6 1BL

Trudy Klauber  

Introduction

The Child Psychotherapist's main work is with children or adolescents individually. Ideally, one hopes that a colleague will support the individual work by working regularly with parents. Apart from regular reviews, the individual work is kept separate with a clear boundary. The patient's privacy is protected, and so is the setting within which the psychotherapist and the patient can work together on understanding the patient's internal reality.

In the case presented here, circumstances did not allow for such a division of labour. As in many Child Guidance Clinics, the Social Workers were under great pressure. They were made to undertake additional, time-consuming statutory work, and were unable to offer frequent, regular work with parents. A little later on, all of them resigned from the clinic within a short space of time. I, the Child Psychotherapist, was left with a young, very disturbed, adolescent patient in twice-weekly psychotherapy and an acute family crisis which threatened this adopted girl's placement with her family. I found myself undertaking weekly family therapy with them, while continuing to see my original patient for her individual sessions.

In this paper, I intend to describe the family work and its impact on the work with the girl, whom I shall call Louise. I have some thoughts about the experience in relation to some of the technical questions which arise over boundaries and about managing the counter-transference. Further questions are addressed about the difficulties in assessing individual pathology, perhaps particularly in cases of adoption, where there is a deprived, bereaved and traumatised family history.

Louise

Louise, who had been adopted at the age of fifteen months, was referred to me by the psychiatrist who had been seeing her since she was five. She had been referred to him by her adoptive parents. They complained that she was impossible at home, and always had been. She would rarely seek affection, and had been constantly active, “like a monkey”, since she came to them. She was rude and difficult with her adoptive mother, and made constant complaints that she was unloved and uncared for. She was destructive with her possessions, which hurt her adoptive parents, sharpening new pencils until they disappeared and damaging many things with scissors.

[[RunningHead]]

Some Thoughts on Eccentricity and Victimization: A Report on the Treatment of a Latency Boy

Tessa Baradon

Tessa Baradon

22 Edmunds Walk
London N2

Tessa Baradon  

Eccentric children often suffer quite brutal treatment at the hands of their peers. What is it in their inner world - conflicts, fantasies, defences - that plays in to the group ostracization? This paper discusses the treatment of a latency boy with a history of “weird” behaviour and bullying at school and in the neighbourhood. The therapy was in a sense a limited intervention since we had one and a half years of twice-weekly treatment before Justin moved away from London with his family. Yet his investment in his “therapy lessons”, as he termed them, facilitated our insight into the dialectic process between the bizarre child and his environment, as well as the inner dilemmas of this unusual and endearing child.

Background

Justin was 11 when his parents emerged from years of despair and pain and took stock of their eldest child. At the time of referral Justin had a long list of miserable symptoms that reached back a long time. His parents described him as withdrawn and in an unhappy world of his own. He was emotional, babyish and sucked his thumb. Bedwetting had stopped only a few years earlier. At the age of 9 Justin was transferred to another school because of severe physical bullying. The problem was alleviated by the change but difficulties with peers continued. Academically he was behind because of problems in concentration and his resistance to change. The parents used the word “weird” to describe his peculiar mannerisms which drew attention and teasing, such as incessant humming and handflapping.

The notion of damage emerged after a traumatic birth when the doctors assured the parents that their baby was not brain-damaged. Because of this the parents felt that everything he did seemed perfect and they indulged him. This “good enough” early infancy is important in light of the later history. When Justin was 3 years old mother suffered the first of a number of miscarriages, until Justin's sister Lily was born when he was 6. The years of attempting to carry through a second pregnancy were fraught with mother's depression, strains in the marriage and financial insecurity, and the parents were relieved by Justin's increasing withdrawal. Lily was unhealthy at birth and therefore the familial strain was not alleviated until a couple of years later. By then the parents questioned whether Justin had been “damaged” by them.

The Normal Child with Disabled Parents: Mary

Caroline Gluckman

Caroline Gluckman

2 Alma Terrace
Allen Street
London W8 6QY.

Caroline Gluckman  

An increasing amount of psychotherapeutic work is being undertaken with physically and mentally disabled children and the literature in this area is usefully expanding. I should like to give some thought to the problem of handicap from the point of view of the normal child who is born to physically handicapped parents, an area that deserves some attention as disabled people are increasingly asserting their right to have children. In recent years two such children have come my way at the clinic where I work. The first was the child of deaf parents who could himself hear normally. He was described by his teacher as “one of the angriest children she had ever met”. My brief and fruitless contact with this boy was passed in an atmosphere of totally silent fury which I was barely able to break through. He quickly refused to come and so it was not possible even to start therapy.

I was naturally, then, interested when another child with disabled parents came my way and I began to wonder if there might be similarities and to think more generally about the problems such children might experience. The new case was a 9-year old girl I shall call Mary of the Green family. Her parents were both physically handicapped with partial paralysis.

The Referral

Mary was officially referred for “anxiety symptoms”: she was pulling her eye-lashes out. This had first happened, it appeared, after mother had expressed some pleasure that she would have some “peace and quiet” when Mary was away at her Nan's. Mary was reported to have been distraught. It turned out that Mary had also once threatened to commit suicide and was very difficult to manage in the mornings using all sorts of delaying tactics about getting dressed and ready. In my initial interview with Mary and her mother it was this slowness in the morning and also stubbornness about homework which were the main complaints. The eye-lashes were only brought up when I asked. Mrs. Green made an interesting comment herself about Mary's approach to life, which she described as non-aggressive in contrast to her little brother, John, who was much more open emotionally: she said “Mary wouldn't lash out”, providing a clue as to the unconscious meaning of this lash pulling which I came to see, indeed, as a way of attacking or “lashing” her parents.

Elizabeth Holder

Elizabeth Holder

Elizabeth Holder  

Psychoanalysis and history are inextricably bound. No-one practising the former can do so without a fine respect for the latter and a firm belief in the influence it exerts on the here and now. So it is both pleasurable and salutary to be firmly reminded from time to time of one's professional links with the past and of its relevance to ongoing work.

For past graduates of the Anna Freud Centre (originally the Hampstead Clinic) this book will be a rewarding encounter with the familiar, akin to re-reading a “family history” that awakens innumerable personal memories. For other readers it will provide insights into some aspects of developmental work with children which have become central to our thinking. It shows how, for instance, the baby observations of today began in Vienna in the 1920s with Charlotte Bühler who constructed developmental profiles of babies from observational studies in which she was helped and trained, both by Ilse Hellman and Esther Bick.

This book is a collaboration between a psychotherapist and a philosopher in the attempt to produce a unified view of the values of psychotherapy. “Confusion of Tongues” Revisited

David Hadley

David Hadley

14 Belgrave Road
Bath BA1 6LU

David Hadley  

Introduction

In this paper I wish to explore the impact of child sexual abuse upon the inner world of the child and trace the implications of this for investigative and therapeutic processes. I shall draw upon two main sources in my thinking around these issues: Ferenczi's paper (Ferenczi 1933) entitled Confusion of tongues between adults and the child - the language of tenderness and of passion, and some therapeutic work with an abused girl, focussing upon one session in detail.

Marie

Marie was 4 and had, by her own report, been interfered with sexually by her father on an access visit. She first told her mother and later others that he had stuck his fingers up inside her bottom and hurt her whilst he was bathing her. Medical examination offered confirmatory physical evidence of damage to the vagina and suggested that penetration had taken place on a number of occasions. A disclosure interview using ‘anatomical’ dolls followed and I was told that this suggested Marie had been penetrated by father's penis, that she had witnessed and possibly been involved in sexual activities of a perverse kind between father and his girlfriend. The level of the child's distress and confusion, however, made it difficult to be sure what had taken place beyond what she had first stated. There was some question as to whether Marie's younger sister had been abused as well, but this was deemed unlikely.

Mother had been separated from Marie's father for two years and, following the disclosure, was persistent in seeking therapeutic help for Marie and herself. She was concerned about Marie's soiling, wetting, nightmares and sleep disturbance since the disclosure. Also she felt out of her depth in knowing how to deal with Marie who was very quickly angered or upset by minor setbacks and found it difficult to accept comfort from her mother.

Father had been interviewed by the police and denied the allegations. Police and social workers were convinced the abuse had taken place but there was insufficient evidence to prosecute. It had been decided that access would be denied to father.

Dorothy Judd

Dorothy Judd

Dorothy Judd  

I have found that professional support for bereaved children is often not available, and that many adults do not understand or acknowledge the grieving process in children.

Parents’ own grief, as well as mutual protectiveness between adults and children, often preclude the possibility of a parent supporting the

112

child and validating the child's feelings. Therefore the provision of a bereavement group for occasions when the normal and essential process of mourning becomes stuck or pathological, and even as a prophylactic facilitator of this process, seems worthwhile.

Upon first looking through this American Bereavement Support Program for Children, I was fearful that it would be an example of the exploitation or commercialisation of death that has emanated from the U.S.A. for over twenty years: part of a culture that can treat death cosmetically, literally in the form of made-up corpses, and metaphorically in Gardens of Rest reminiscent of children's fantasies of Heaven.

However, this package completely avoids the dangers of euphemism and idealisation. Indeed, it is an honest, serious, and successful attempt to provide a useful pack for group leaders, consisting of a Leader's manual, and a separate participant's workbook. Thus, they suggest that two leaders conduct a five-week programme, for a group of bereaved 5-10 year-olds, and, separately, for the 11 - 15 range. They discuss the size and composition of groups, and consider whether the circumstances of the death need affect eligibility for a group. They do not exclude children bereaved through the suicide of a parent or close relative. They discuss the length of time since the death, the need for parent/guardian cooperation, and other considerations in planning such a group. They pay attention to the possibility of abnormal grief reactions, and suggest when further professional help be sought.

I found much material that was useful and interesting.

Using the Positive: Is the Truth Always the Awful Truth?

Susan Kegerreis

Susan Kegerreis

67 Addison Gardens
London W14 ODT

Susan Kegerreis  

Introduction

Recent articles by Kleinian-trained psychotherapists seem to show a resurgence of attention paid to the positive: a new, or perhaps I should say renewed, interest in the forces for good in the personality and the possible benignity of mental processes rather than in pathology and destructiveness.

For example, in her paper Beyond the Unpleasure Principle, Anne Alvarez (1988) asks us to look more carefully at the ways in which play contains the hopes and aspirations of children, and their capacity to have fun, rather than stressing only the way in which play is the evasion of reality.

Meira Likierman (1988) invites us to look at a little emphasised aspect of maternal psychic nourishment for the infant: mother's primitive, narcissistic positive projective identification that gives the baby an important experience of love and goodness being put into him.

In a different way, Anne Alvarez's paper on Latency (1989) is also in this category, by emphasising the healthy use of defences, the protective function of mechanisms which are very often, she seems to imply, automatically taken to be pathological and as needing to be removed in the analysis. She stresses that defences are at times necessary steps on the way to inner strength. (A telling example given in supervision was to look at a little boy's attempt to build a tower not as a defensive illusion that he was big and strong, but as a way of saying, “At least here I can have a go at being big and strong”.)

When I first heard or read these papers, it has to be admitted that amongst my appreciation I experienced some disquiet at the apparent assumption that Kleinian therapists would naturally see these positive elements very differently. There seemed to be an underlying assumption about “Kleinians” that was disturbing. Were we really not able to value the fun in play, to see the positive trying-out of roles rather than just the evasion of grim reality? Were we not aware that babies needed their mothers to idealise them and fill them with their own good feelings? Was it really supposed that we did not realise that defences were necessary and helpful at times?

The Foot in the Hole in the Dress: The Development and Use of Symbols in the Psychotherapy of an Eleven Year Old Girl**

Jenny Kenrick

Jenny Kenrick

43 Lamont Road
London SW10 0HS

Jenny Kenrick  

Throughout the course of seven years of three times weekly psychotherapy one thing has been without question: Livia, an eleven year old Afro-Caribbean girl, has wanted urgently to communicate the quality of her internal world. It was this urgency that got through to Children's Home staff when she came into care aged three and a half. She and her brother of one and a half had been neglected and, in Livia's case, abused by their schizophrenic mother. They had been received into care several times but finally became subject to Care Orders after neighbours had heard Livia's cries and had seen her head jammed through a broken window. The mother had left the children to go to her evening class in computing. In the Children's Home it was found Livia could neither feed herself, nor play, nor sleep unless first tied down in her cot. She was either in a state of restless activity, or thumb in mouth she clung onto a member of staff. Much affected by her state, they referred her to a Department of Child Psychiatry for help, and a year later she started psychotherapy with me. By that time her legal status had been decided and, as a result of containment and consistency of care in the Children's Home, she was able to play and her language was well developed.

The therapeutic work which then began was characterised by a process which Bion described as the interplay between the container and the contained. His theory of development, and in particular of the development of thinking, derives from the model of the infant/mother relationship. The infant projects into the mother the emotions that he/she is still too immature to have developed any means to process. The infant requires a mother, who, drawing on her own internal object, is capable of receiving and processing the emotions in such a way that the infant is not overwhelmed by them. The mother is offering her baby what Bion calls alpha function. This function can be experienced by the infant as that which Bion called a “thinking breast” which, when all is working well between mother and infant, enables the infant to develop its own object. A prime task of that object is the creation of “symbols” (in Bion's sense of the term), without which thinking cannot take place. Bion drew attention to projective identification as a basic mode of communication between infant and mother, and thus as the infant's first tool in establishing the complex process of the development of symbols for thinking.

Defences of the Self in a Pre-Adolescent Boy**

Miranda Davies

Miranda Davies

53 Marlborough Crescent
London W4 1HG

Miranda Davies  

Introduction

I should like to discuss the early, primitive defences that I came up against in the treatment of a boy whom I saw for analysis when he was 10 to 12 years of age. I came to understand these as his defences of the self, defences of a kind that presented a particular difficulty in the analytic work. So far in the development of a working model of the psyche, we have, broadly speaking, two main categories of defence: ego defences, and the primitive infantile defences that underlie them. The ego defences were delineated by Freud and further elaborated by Anna Freud in The Ego and Mechanisms of Defence (A. Freud, 1937); they include regression, repression, reaction-formation, isolation, undoing, projection, introjection, turning against the self and reversal. Klein distinguished a sub-group of more primitive defence mechanisms used against early infantile anxieties of a psychotic nature, such as fear of death by falling to pieces (disintegration) or being crushed by annihilating forces. These are splitting, idealization, denial, and projective and introjective identification. It is these primitive defences that Fordham explores in his paper Defences of the self where he writes that, “in the case of part objects there is no unconsciousness, but rather more or less violent attempts to attack and do away with the bad object - they can reach a level at which one must speak in terms of annihilation. It is in this area that total defences are mobilized” Fordham, (1974, p. 153). Fordham has called these total defences “defences of the self” and the difference between Klein's primitive infantile defences and Fordham's defences of the self is quantitative: defences of the self are more extreme, they are total. A definition by Lambert is helpful here.

Although the distinction is by no means absolute, it is still possible to distinguish between a kind of half-blind defence against annihilation of the personality as such and defences that are involved in protecting the ego-consciousness from the experience of pain of all sorts.

Susan Reid

Susan Reid

Susan Reid  

This book is a companion volume to Tustin's previous book, Autistic Barriers in Neurotic Patients (1987) and includes some revised papers previously published.

The first chapter describes the development of thinking about autism from Kanner in 1943 through to the present day and covers the ideas of psychoanalytic writers as well as writers with other theoretical constructs. The second chapter outlines the understanding gained from studying autistic children in the therapeutic situation, whilst Chapters 3, 4 and 5 concentrate on psychotherapy. Chapter 6 presents detailed material from Tustin's clinical work with David who, she says, taught her about “autistic encapsulation”; whilst Chapters 7 and 8 open the field to the exploration of the “autistic capsule” in adult patients and seek to demonstrate how the findings from therapeutic work with autistic patients have wider applications in our work with neurotic patients, children and adults. Chapter 9 returns to John, a patient about whom Tustin has written before, who taught Tustin about the “black hole”. The clinical material presented here is from later sessions to illustrate the progress in psychotherapy. Chapter 10 is based on the work of three Chilean psychoanalysts who give clinical material from an adult male patient to illustrate how the patient's rich language was not in the service of communication but was, rather, like the autistic child's use of autistic objects. Chapters 11 and 12 are brief concluding statements.

The stated focus for this book is the protective function of autism in children whose autism Tustin terms “psychogenic autism”: that is, where psychogenic factors seem to have been most operative. Tustin's present position is that autism may arise in several different situations but it is where the autism is a reaction to what is experienced by the child as a traumatic situation where Tustin has felt able successfully to offer psychotherapy. The children whom Tustin describes have experienced “unbearably sudden and painful awareness of bodily separateness from a mother with whose body they had previously felt fused and equated”. The autism then becomes a protective but impenetrable covering to shut out this unbearable awareness. Tustin emphasises that she has relinquished the term “autism” for an early stage of infantile development and reserves the term autism now to refer only to pathological states. She gives credit for this awareness to the studies of infancy by writers such as Stern (1986), Brazelton (1970), Trevarthen (1979) and Bower (1978) who, she states, have shown us that, in normal development, there are periods of alert awareness. Whilst we all feel indebted to such writers for substantiating our own findings in infant observation, I was disappointed that Tustin had not already found this evidence in the infant observations that our profession has undertaken for many years.

Monica Lanyado

Monica Lanyado

56 Albany Street
Edinburgh EH1 3QR

Monica Lanyado  

Preface

At the risk of stating the obvious, I would like to preface this paper by saying that psychoanalytic psychotherapy with disturbed patients is an extremely difficult and arduous process. Particularly when working in the NHS, with its increasingly stretched resources, psychoanalytically trained psychotherapists tend to see patients from the most extreme end of the spectrum of referrals. The pressures that these patients put on us and our way of working need frankly to be acknowledged and recognised by setting realistic and often limited treatment objectives. It is important to bear these considerations in mind constantly, so as not to become disheartened or surprised when faced with what at times seems to be insurmountable obstacles in the path of psychic change. In the light of the severity of many patients’ histories and presenting problems, it would be naive to expect otherwise.

Introduction

There are many occasions in clinical practice when the problem of “what to do” (within which I am including verbal doing), as opposed to understanding the question of “why”, raises great uncertainty in the therapist. I suspect that work with children and adolescents is particularly difficult in this respect as frequently so much of the analytic process is embodied in the manner in which the basic boundaries of the sessions are upheld, and then challenged by the patients. The therapists’ actions are more likely to be understood than their words. This puts an increased emphasis on the importance of many issues which could easily be regarded as matters of management rather than being central to the analytic process itself. What we actually “do” has to be distilled from clinical experience as well as from the theory which stimulates our thinking and understanding.

In this paper I would like to discuss the many questions that have been raised for me in the treatment of a sexually perverse child. These questions have made me wonder about the appropriateness of “classical” technique (as primarily developed for work with neurotic children) in work with severely traumatised and abused children.

[[RunningHead]]

Interpretations That Feel Horrible to Make and a Theoretical Unicorn**

Valerie Sinason

Valerie Sinason

3 Honeybourne Road
NW6 1HH

Valerie Sinason  

In the last few years I have slowly recognised a cluster of interpretations that I find horrible to make. They are all concerned with trauma: sexual or physical abuse, handicap, fragility and death. They all reflect a clear unbearable external reality. For me to make them involves dealing with blows to my omnipotent wishes to heal, facing cowardice, helplessness, guilt, and a struggle with stupidity and blindness. These interpretations are difficult because they deal with my own fear, not only a fear that comes from a counter-transference experience.

Juliet Hopkins (1986) expresses this clearly in her paper Solving the mystery of monsters: steps towards the recovery from trauma - “It seems that helping a child to recover from trauma is liable to involve the therapist not only in sharing the pain but in suffering grave doubts about whether facing pain so starkly is necessary, and whether the self protection of turning a blind eye may be preferable”.

The problem of dealing with a blind eye applies equally to the internal and external aspects of both therapist and the child. If the child does not want to see because seeing will reveal the awfulness of his predicament, the therapist in seeing must see not only the predicament of the child but also her own areas of difficulty and the theoretical structure that either does or does not support her. In this paper I would like first to explore some theories about interpretations and then provide clinical examples of the particular interpretations I have found hardest to make.

Theory About Interpretations: Mythical or Shifting?

In some ways, psychoanalytical theory is experienced as parental and inconsistencies or myths about different kinds of interpretations can provoke internal dissent and anxiety. Thoughts about a hierarchy of interpretations can play a powerful hidden part in influencing what we see and can't see. Knowing what we are not supposed to know (Bowlby, 1979) affects the therapist as much as the child. If we “know” a certain kind of interpretation is regarded more highly in our own internalised theoretical orthodoxy, that will influence the words we use.

Maria Pozzi

Maria Pozzi

65, Holly Lodge Mansions
Highgate - London N6 6HD

Maria Pozzi  

M.P.: In the last four years during your supervisions and my subsequent regular visits to you in Amersham, I have learnt many things about you and your life, which have both fascinated me and helped me in my own personal as well as professional life. You spent the first supervision in getting to know me: that was the first task you had to accomplish for you to be able to tune in better both with supervisees and with the patient that was going to be discussed. You offered then to give me a “double time” and that was not the only occasion. This was my first taste of your generosity and good-heartedness. You have shown me that your life and your work have never been separate and that they have been a whole and a continuum, just like your supervisions. I would like to ask you something about your early life, your family, your father, your mother and your relationship with them.

ET.: Well, now, my parents were both very religious people. They were engaged in professional jobs in the Church of England. My father was a lay reader, who then became an army padre in the First World War. He was a very fine speaker and a very fine preacher, just like my mother was, but he was a very unconventional man. My father's antecedents on his mother's side had been Quakers. When he was a prisoner in a German prison war camp, he lost his religious faith because he became critical of the Church's attitude to war. He became a pacifist. When he returned to England he left the Church and trained as a teacher. He was very interested in progressive education and in the work of A.S. Neill. On one occasion my father and I visited Summerhill and stayed for a week. Neill offered my father a job which he could not take because my mother was shocked by Neill's ideas. My father then ran a village school, according to the ideas of A.S. Neill, which I attended. So I had my father as a teacher for a time.

My mother came from a much more conventional background. She trained as a Church Sister, a deaconess, in a posh training school in Chelsea and she was always called “Sister Minnie”. She disapproved of Neill's ideas because he had been psychoanalised by Wilhelm Reich. I'm sure that she would have thought that psychoanalysis was wicked. This is what she thought of most of my father's ideas when they were both engaged in Church work. She thought my father was wicked because he didn't believe in the Virgin Birth. Moreover he would read authors like Bernard Shaw. My father was a socialist, an anarchist, whereas my mother was High Tory. So as you can see, I was brought up in a very argumentative atmosphere.

Adrian Sutton  

Introduction

In recent years the plight of abused and severely deprived children has come far more into both professional and public awareness. Increased recognition and improvements in response have occurred, although serious and considerable pitfalls remain (Butler-Sloss 1988). However, the provision of suitable alternative homes and treatment, including psychotherapy, for those who require these remains scarce and problematic. In the United Kingdom, psychotherapy services for children are poor: there are few trained Child Psychotherapists and their distribution leaves large areas of the country without any at all (Association of Child Psychotherapy 1989). Training in psychoanalytic psychotherapy short of a full training is also scarce (Royal College of Psychiatrists, in press). Providing therapeutic treatment for children will require two steps: an increase in the number of therapists and a movement outwards from established centres. The latter will ensure that individuals move away from their previous professional institutions to develop a culture in which therapy can be carried out, and to provide such therapy.

This paper describes some of the experiences and issues which have arisen for me in the treatment of a severely deprived young boy who was my first psychotherapy patient on moving from my training institution to take up the post of Consultant Child Psychiatrist in another part of the country. In relation to the child, this has been a process of helping him to develop new ways of viewing the world and his relationships, giving up some of the ways which had resulted from his own severe deprivation and which had only served to perpetuate his emotional isolation. For me, part of the process has been the negotiation of an experience of loss (of the previous psychoanalytic culture) along what can be considered “a normal professional developmental path”. The process has been one of attempting to create and maintain an environment conducive to psychotherapy within the physical setting and institutional culture, and also within myself as the child's therapist. The complications which can arise when these processes occur simultaneously are at the heart of this paper.

Priscilla Roth

Priscilla Roth

Priscilla Roth  

This work is a major achievement, both in its content and in its form. The two volumes contain a large number of important papers which ought to be a part of the intellectual background of everyone seriously concerned with psycho-analysis. The books trace the development of several of Mrs. Klein's concepts through the work of some of her followers over the last thirty years; Mrs. Spillius makes it clear that she has specifically focused on those aspects of Mrs. Klein's work which have particularly interested and generated research by Kleinian psychoanalysts in Britain. Within these self-imposed limits, Mrs. Spillius does a masterful job of clarifying Kleinian thinking - demonstrating developments arising from Mrs. Klein's ideas and also suggesting possible future developments and areas of interest.

What distinguishes the book immediately is its form. The papers are presented schematically so that what we have is not in any sense merely a collection of articles but a carefully laid out diagram of the development of Kleinian ideas and theories. The result is a map drawn by an editor utterly familiar with the terrain, its difficulties as well as its beauty spots, who can point out which trails have become main roads which have yet to be developed, at which points divergences have occurred, and where what once looked like a highway seems, for the moment anyway, to have disappeared into the woods.

The work is made up of two volumes: Mainly Theory and Mainly Practice. There is a General Introduction to the entire collection at the beginning of the first volume, and then each section within each volume is preceded by its own Introduction describing what is to come, giving a brief precis of each of the papers and spelling out some of the connections between them. Mrs. Spillius also describes how each section - that is, each theme she is exploring - links to the others. This method is extremely clarifying - I finished each group of papers feeling I had an increased and more coherent understanding of the subject and could connect it with ideas presented in previous section.

Mara Sidoli: The Unfolding Self. Sigo Press. 1990 (£4.95).

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson  

In this book, Maria Sidoli offers us a richly evocative clinical account of the processes of separation and individuation - the unfolding self in infancy. She is influenced by Michael Fordham's thinking. He, in turn, though coming from a Jungian background, has himself been profoundly influenced by Melanie Klein and Bion, so that his writings are a distillation of his own clinical insights, his loyalty to Jung and his recognition of the value of Kleinian developments for work in child analysis. Mara Sidoli tries to synthesise his formulations and shows how they underpin her clinical observations. This book offers the reader the opportunity to examine these ideas via detailed accounts of mother-baby observation and descriptions of psychotherapy with young children, adolescents and adults. These are all linked to the main theme of the unfolding self and the difficulties in subsequent development that result from early mother-infant dysfunctions and failures in early bonding. The strength of the book lies in her descriptions of these clinical observations. They are vivid, written with honesty and are often quite poetic.

There are several problems, however. In the first place one feels the writer to be struggling to address several theories of development at the same time. Jungian ideas are not always spelt out sufficiently well enough for the non Jungian reader to assimilate easily and both Jung and Fordham are examined, discussed and defined by quoting ideas from both their own and Kleinian writings as though all the different models were saying the same thing. This leads to confused conceptualisation and does nothing to enhance or extend her exploration of her way of working and her ideas are in danger of becoming ideological flags.

Sidoli follows Fordham's theory of the Primal Self. Fordham believes that it is a “steady state of integration” from which the child's ego and body growth will unfold thorugh dynamic processes he termed “deintegration-reintegration”. During deintegrated states “the search for the breast (mother) begins to be experienced as something distinct and not arising from inside the primal self”. This describes a primitive awareness of separateness which, Sidoli suggests, is made tolerable only if the infant is able to bring about a reintegration. In order to describe reintegration Sidoli quotes Frances Tustin who suggests that “in early infantile development there is an awareness of separateness which is made tolerable in the baby by auto-sensuous activities and bodily interactions with other people, especially mother”. Understanding of reintegration has to be arrived at by the reader through the clinical descriptions. These seem to imply that it is about the capacity of the baby to recover the link with the mother, who, in turn, supports that potential by her own capacity to metabolise her infant's communications and distress. (Here Sidoli seems to be incorporating Bion's thinking).

Reflections on the Process of Internalisation**

Gianna Williams

Gianna Williams

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3

Gianna Williams  

I would like to reflect in this paper on some aspects of the process of internalisation. I refer to the beginning of the internalisation of “an object that loves and protects the self” (Klein 1957) described by Melanie Klein as the basic source of inner strength.

I will describe the first two years of work with David, a boy who was eighteen years old when he referred himself to the Tavistock. He was severely disabled as he was born without arms from the elbow down. Only after two years of treatment was he able to let go of the grip of his eyes on me and began using the couch. I thought it would be pertinent to the subject of this paper to describe the development of our relationship during those first two years.

David

David referred himself to the Tavistock Young People's Counselling Service and he knew that the service offered only up to four sessions. He said, on the phone, that a teacher at his college had advised him to get in touch with us because he thought he might have problems and it might be helpful for him to talk to a counsellor. In the telephone call he made no mention of his disability. He repeated to me, in the first session, that he did not really know why he had decided to ask for an appointment. It had been his tutor's idea. He was attending the first year of an art foundation course and he enjoyed college and enjoyed living in the halls. He launched into a description of his work, of his painting and there was no mention of any problem.

He was very articulate, appeared very sure of himself and put across the feeling he would be very happy if I did not ask any questions. This handsome boy, looking at me with very gripping eyes, was sitting with his stumps held behind the back of the couch, his legs crossed, ear phones around his neck and a walkman clipped to his belt, a lively engaging adolescent, talking about his love for painting. From time to time he would brush his forehead and pull his hair back with his right stump, with a very natural movement, as if passing a hand through his hair.

Chriso Andreou

51 Harberton Road

Chriso Andreou  

Introduction

In this paper I would like to discuss my experience of working with a severely disturbed girl. I hope to show, through clinical material, the nature and intensity of the transference relationship. I also hope to demonstrate the effects of early emotional deprivation as shown through her sense of abandonment and the influence that the trauma of sexual abuse had on the development of her sexuality.

Background

The information that I have of Mary's background and family history is very sketchy, limited to the main events in her life as recorded by Social Services. How she experienced them and the secret she kept were later revealed in therapy.

She was born to a very young mother who soon abandoned her child to be looked after by her grandmother. At the age of 3 Mary was received into care due to physical neglect and placed in a residential nursery. A year later she was fostered and was said to be happy and settled until she was nine years old. At that time she started to become physically and verbally aggressive at home and at school and started to steal. Her foster parents said that they could not manage her any longer. She was moved and placed in a children's home. Further attempts to foster her failed as she herself always rejected the prospective foster parents. She was seen by the adults who cared for her as a very complex girl, very loyal to those she felt deserved her loyalty but totally scathing of those who did not meet her high standards. She liked her school and was very attached to one of her teachers who was very supportive towards her. She refused any contact with her family and expressed hatred towards her mother who embarrassed her and whom she thought of as a prostitute and a drunk.

Referral for Psychotherapy

Her Social Worker referred her for psychotherapy to NAFSYAT (The Intercultural Therapy Centre) when she was 16 years old. Her Social Worker's main anxiety was about Mary's preoccupation with suicidal thoughts and her depression. She was also concerned about her hateful expressions towards her mother and extreme violent feelings, for example, saying that she wanted to kill her mother. She expressed dislike and disgust about the colour of her skin and projected her violent feelings towards a black residential Social Worker whom she called thick and stupid.

Tom Main: The Ailment and other Psychoanalytic Essays. Edited by Jennifer Johns. Published by Free Association Books, 1989. Hardback, £27.50.

Deborah Bellman

Deborah Bellman

Deborah Bellman  

Born in 1911 and dying in 1990, shortly after the publication of this book, Tom Main was a man whose energy, creativity, and pioneering spirit infused his life, his work, and his writings. Best known, perhaps, as Medical Director of the Cassel Hospital from 1946-1976, he had previously worked in army psychiatry during the war, and later, in the ‘70s, was instrumental in founding the Institute of Psychosexual Medicine, of which he was Life President. A psychoanalyst, he was passionately committed to the applications of psychoanalysis, and to the understanding of the workings of different social systems.

Tom Main's writings were numerous, and the task of selection for this volume must have been onerous. Whatever the complexities of the task, the result of Jennifer Johns’ work is a collection of essays that are beautifully coherent, and that vividly convey the development of many of the author's ideas. The papers are of both historical and contemporary interest, and together with Eric Rayner's excellent introduction, make for stimulating, exciting, and enjoyable reading.

For those who, like me, have often skimmed through an introduction, impatient to get on with ‘the book’, it is worth emphasising that this one merits a closer look. In it, Eric Rayner, himself introduced to psychoanalysis by Tom Main, both imparts a lively sense of Tom Main's forceful, passionate and compassionate character and puts the paper into a social and historical context. We learn how, for example, benefitting from Bion's experience of the Northfield Experiment (an army psychiatric hospital), Tom Main began to develop his own ideas about the hospital as a therapeutic institution when he himself worked at Northfield. These ideas came into fruition once at the Cassel Hospital, where he developed the idea of a therapeutic community. For Tom Main, the essence of a therapeutic community lay in the self-scrutinizing process: in the individual, between people, and within and between different levels of an organisation. This idea, and many others set forth in the introduction, resonate throughout the book.
